function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **complete, ready‑to‑use set of files** that you can drop into the `nodejs-welcome` repository.  
After adding them, just commit and push – the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically build the Docker image whenever you push to `main`.

> **NOTE**  
> I can’t actually clone or push to the repo from here, but the instructions below will get you up and running in minutes.

---

## 1. Clone the repository (if you haven’t already)

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2. Repository analysis (quick recap)

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `package.json` | Node.js dependencies & scripts |
| `app.js` (or similar) | Entry point of the application |
| `README.md` | Project documentation |
| `LICENSE` | Licensing information |

The app listens on **port 3000** (the default for many Node.js starter projects).  
We’ll build a lightweight Docker image (`node:18-alpine`) and expose that port.

---

## 3. Create / update the Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` at the root of the repo:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Base image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Metadata
LABEL maintainer="Unknown"

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why `node:18-alpine`?**  
> It’s small, secure, and includes the latest LTS Node.js runtime.

---

## 4. Create Kubernetes YAML files

Create a directory `k8s/` and add `deployment.yaml` inside it:

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- change if you use another registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deployment: 2 replicas of the container.  
> * Service: Exposes the pods on port 80 inside the cluster (you can change to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` if you need external access).

---

## 5. GitHub Actions workflow

Create the directory `.github/workflows/` and add `ci.yml`:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI – Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Set up Docker Buildx
      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      # Log in to GitHub Container Registry (ghcr.io)
      - name: Log in to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build and push the image
      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest
          # Optional: add a short SHA tag
          # tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest,ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}

      # Optional: create a GitHub release (uncomment if you want releases)
      # - name: Create Release
      #   uses: softprops/action-gh-release@v2
      #   with:
      #     tag_name: v${{ github.run_number }}
      #     generate_release_notes: true
```

### What the workflow does

1. **Trigger** on pushes to `main`.  
2. Checks out the repo.  
3. Sets up Docker Buildx (multi‑platform support).  
4. Logs into GitHub Container Registry using the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN`.  
5. Builds the Docker image from the root `Dockerfile` and pushes it to `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest`.  
6. (Optional) You can add a release step if you’d like to tag releases automatically.

> **Important** – The workflow uses the default `GITHUB_TOKEN`, which has permission to push to the same repository’s container registry. No extra secrets are required.

---

## 6. Add, commit, and push the changes

```bash
# Stage all new/updated files
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml

# Commit
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# Push to main
git push origin main
```

Once the push completes, GitHub Actions will automatically start the build.  
You can verify the workflow run in the **Actions** tab of your repository.

---

## 7. Verify the Docker image

After the workflow finishes, you can inspect the image on GitHub Container Registry:

```
ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

You can pull it locally to test:

```bash
docker pull ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
docker run -p 3000:3000 ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

Open `http://localhost:3000` to confirm the app is running.

---

### Recap of the files added

| Path | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node.js image |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deployment + Service for Kubernetes |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | CI pipeline that builds & pushes the Docker image |

That’s it! Your repo now has a fully automated Docker build pipeline and ready‑to‑deploy Kubernetes manifests. Happy coding!
